notable_claims: Resource accounting packages on large computers allow universities to itemize the costs of email and news.
Ambiguous terms like 'incremental cost' in rights definitions can lead to misinterpretation by both users and administration.
The author suggests that Usenet content may be more appropriate for public libraries than university environments.
organizations: State University of New York, Stony Brook
classification.summary: Sanjay Kapur critiques a proposed list of electronic rights for university members, questioning the ambiguity of terms like 'incremental cost' and 'small.' He discusses the distinction between resource allocation and censorship, specifically regarding Usenet newsgroups. Additionally, he suggests that public libraries might be more appropriate venues for Usenet access than universities.
classification.title: Re: Which Rights?

notable_claims: Privacy rights for electronic files are comparable to the privacy of physical office desks.
Members of a university community do not surrender their constitutional rights of privacy by joining the academic community.
Search warrants should be required before searching offices or living quarters assigned to individuals.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that privacy rights for electronic files should be analogous to the privacy of physical desks and offices. He cites university student codes and ACLU guidance on Fourth Amendment rights to argue against the notion that public university employees forfeit all privacy regarding their work documents.
classification.title: RE: Which rights?

notable_claims: The author seeks to build a cogent case for why email should be private.
classification.summary: Allan H. Levy requested that university members share their institutions' formal email privacy policies. He specifically sought to distinguish the issue of email privacy from the censorship of bulletin boards. The request was sent to a mailing list and copied to Carl Kadie at the Electronic Frontier Foundation.
classification.title: email privacy policies at universities??

notable_claims: Newsgroups are more similar to mail or speech than to a curated library collection.
University systems should prioritize newsgroups that relate to the organization's academic mission when disk space is limited.
classification.summary: Joe Brennan discusses the parallels and differences between library collection management and the curation of Usenet newsgroups on university systems. He argues that while libraries must make value judgments due to physical space constraints, digital newsfeeds are more akin to speech or mail. He suggests that if disk space is limited, universities should prioritize groups related to their academic mission over high-volume, non-academic content.
classification.title: Re: Which Rights?

notable_claims: Newsgroups function as serials/periodicals and are thus covered by library policies like the ALA's Freedom To Read statement.
Some electronic journals on Usenet and Bitnet have been assigned ISSN numbers.
sci.psychology.digest was recognized as one of the best new magazines of 1990 by Library Journal.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie argues that Usenet newsgroups should be classified as serials or periodicals rather than mere communication tools. He contends that this classification brings them under the protection of existing library policies and the American Library Association's 'Freedom To Read' statement. The post provides evidence of electronic journals receiving ISSN numbers and professional recognition from Library Journal.
classification.title: Re: Which Rights?

notable_claims: A newsgroup system is functionally a library.
Administrators making subscription decisions for others are acting as librarians regardless of their degree.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to Sanjay Kapur's suggestion that newsgroups should be managed by libraries rather than computing facilities. Kadie argues that the library is a distributed network rather than a monolithic entity and asserts that anyone managing newsgroup subscriptions is effectively acting as a librarian. He urges computer science administrators to respect and defend users' Freedom to Read.
classification.title: Which Rights?

notable_claims: A newsgroup system can be viewed as a library.
System administrators making subscription decisions are effectively acting as librarians.
Computer scientists and programmers are not trained to manage the ethical responsibilities of defending a user's freedom to read.
organizations: State University of New York, Stony Brook
classification.summary: A debate regarding whether system administrators should be responsible for upholding the 'Freedom to Read' when managing newsgroup subscriptions. Carl Kadie argues that anyone making subscription decisions acts as a librarian; Sanjay Kapur counters that programmers and system administrators lack the professional training of librarians and should not be burdened with these ethical responsibilities.
classification.title: Re: Which Rights?

notable_claims: University computing policies are often heavy on prohibitions and light on permissions.
Institutional policy typically evolves from informal to proscriptive, then toward a balance of rights and responsibilities.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie argues that university computing policies typically evolve from no policy to overly proscriptive regulations, and finally to a balance of rights and responsibilities. To illustrate this pattern, he provides a detailed historical case study of student conduct regulations at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign from 1904 to 1973. He suggests that understanding this general institutional evolution can help guide the development of academic computer policy.
classification.title: From Regulations to Rights: The Maturation of Policy

notable_claims: The NCSA Director could order searches of user disk space for email that 'attempted to disadvantage NCSA'.
Computer professionals viewed such restrictive email policies as highly unpopular.
classification.summary: Paul Pomes discusses the restrictive computer policies at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) at the University of Illinois. He highlights a policy allowing the NCSA Director to search user disk space if email is suspected of disadvantaging the center. Pomes describes efforts to pressure the organization by informing potential job applicants about these policies.
classification.title: Re: From Regulations to Rights: The Mat
